items.stem: The law of reflection states that …
options: the angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
the angle of reflection is always 45°
items.answer: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
items.markingKey: Both measured from the normal.

items.stem: Explain why the image in a plane mirror is described as virtual.
items.answer: The reflected rays do not actually pass through the image position; they only appear to come from a point behind the mirror, so it cannot be put on a screen.
items.markingKey: rays appear to come from behind mirror [1]; cannot be shown on screen [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why "AMBULANCE" is written in reverse on the front of ambulances.
items.answer: Drivers see it in their rear-view mirrors, which laterally invert the image, so it reads correctly.
items.markingKey: lateral inversion [1]; reads correctly in mirror [1] [2]

items.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 70°. Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray.
Yusuf stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror and then walks 1 m towards it. Calculate the distance between them and their image before and after, and describe two other properties of the image.
items.answer: Before 4 m; after 2 m. The image is virtual, upright, same size, laterally inverted.
items.markingKey: image distance = object distance [1]; 4 m and 2 m [1]; two properties [1] [3]

items.stem: Mohammed stands 1.5 m in front of a large plane mirror in a dance studio. (a) A ray from the person’s shoe meets the mirror at 35° to the normal. State its angle of reflection. (b) Explain why the image cannot be formed on a screen. (c) The person moves 0.5 m closer. State the new distance between person and image.
items.answer: (a) 35° (b) Rays do not actually meet there; they only appear to come from behind the mirror. (c) 2 m
items.markingKey: (a) 35° [1] (b) Rays do not actually meet there [1]; they only appear to come from behind the mirror [1] [2] (c) 2 m [1]

items.stem: Describe how to verify the law of reflection using a ray box and a plane mirror.
items.answer: Draw a normal on paper at the mirror; direct rays at different angles of incidence; mark incident and reflected rays; measure both angles from the normal with a protractor and compare.
items.markingKey: normal drawn [1]; several angles measured with protractor [1]; compare i and r [1] [3]

items.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle between the incident and reflected rays?
A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray.
Priya stands 1 m in front of a plane mirror and then walks 0.5 m towards it. Calculate the distance between them and their image before and after, and describe two other properties of the image.
items.answer: Before 2 m; after 1 m. The image is virtual, upright, same size, laterally inverted.
items.markingKey: image distance = object distance [1]; 2 m and 1 m [1]; two properties [1] [3]

items.stem: When light passes from air into glass, it …
options: does not change direction at any angle
speeds up and bends away from the normal
slows down and bends towards the normal
slows down and bends away from the normal
items.answer: slows down and bends towards the normal
items.markingKey: Glass is optically denser: lower speed, ray bends towards the normal.

items.stem: Explain why a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.
items.answer: Light from the bottom refracts away from the normal as it leaves the water; the eye traces the rays back in straight lines, so they appear to come from a shallower point.
items.markingKey: refraction away from normal at surface [1]; eye traces back in straight line → apparent depth [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe an experiment to measure the refractive index of a glass block.
items.answer: Shine a ray at a measured angle of incidence onto the block; mark the emergent ray; join entry and exit points to find the refracted ray; measure r from the normal; repeat for several i; plot sin i against sin r; gradient = n.
items.markingKey: measure i and r with protractor [1]; repeat for several angles [1]; n = sin i/sin r or gradient [1] [3]

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into glass. The angle of incidence is 65° and the angle of refraction is 37°. Calculate the refractive index.
items.markingKey: n = sin 65° / sin 37° = 1.51. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into diamond (refractive index 2.42) with an angle of incidence of 25°. Calculate the angle of refraction.

A student shines rays into a block of glass. With i = 25° she measures r = 16.4°; with i = 50° she measures r = 30.7°. (a) Calculate the refractive index from each reading. (b) State the mean value. (c) Explain why the ray bends towards the normal on entering the block.
items.answer: (a) 1.5 and 1.5 (b) 1.5 (c) light slows down in glass, which is optically denser than air.
items.markingKey: (a) n = sin i/sin r for each [2] (b) mean [1] (c) slows down in denser medium [1] [4]

items.stem: A ray of light in air strikes a parallel-sided block of crown glass (n = 1.52) at an angle of incidence of 60°. (a) State the angle at which the ray leaves the opposite parallel face, measured from the normal. (b) Explain why the ray changes direction at the first face. (c) Describe how the path would differ if the ray entered along the normal.
items.answer: (a) 60° (b) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle. (c) It would pass straight through without bending.
items.markingKey: (a) 60° [1] (b) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (c) It would pass straight through without bending [1]

items.stem: A ray of light in air strikes a parallel-sided block of water (n = 1.33) at an angle of incidence of 50°. (a) State the angle at which the ray leaves the opposite parallel face, measured from the normal. (b) Explain why the ray changes direction at the first face. (c) State what happens to the frequency of the light inside the block. (d) Describe how the path would differ if the ray entered along the normal.
items.answer: (a) 50° (b) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle. (c) Unchanged. (d) It would pass straight through without bending.
items.markingKey: (a) 50° [1] (b) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (c) Unchanged [1] (d) It would pass straight through without bending [1]

items.stem: Explain why a ray emerging from a parallel-sided glass block is parallel to the incident ray.
items.answer: Refraction at the two parallel faces is equal and opposite, so the ray is displaced sideways but its direction is restored.
items.markingKey: equal and opposite bending [1]; lateral displacement only [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a material with a higher refractive index bends light more.
items.answer: Light slows more in it, so the change in speed at the boundary is greater, causing a larger change of direction.
items.markingKey: greater slowing [1]; larger deviation [1] [2]

items.stem: A ray enters water (n = 1.33) and quartz (n = 1.54) from air at the same angle of incidence of 40°. State in which material it bends more and explain.
items.answer: Quartz: higher refractive index, so light slows more and bends more towards the normal (smaller angle of refraction).
items.markingKey: correct material [1]; higher n → more slowing / smaller r [1] [2]

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into ice. The angle of incidence is 40° and the angle of refraction is 29°. Calculate the refractive index.
items.markingKey: n = sin 40° / sin 29° = 1.33. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ray of light in air strikes a parallel-sided block of crown glass (n = 1.52) at an angle of incidence of 30°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction inside the block. (b) State the angle at which the ray leaves the opposite parallel face, measured from the normal. (c) Describe how the path would differ if the ray entered along the normal.
items.answer: (a) 19.2° (b) 30° (c) It would pass straight through without bending.
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n (method/substitution) [1]; answer 19.2° with unit [1] [2] (b) 30° [1] (c) It would pass straight through without bending [1]

items.stem: A ray of light in air strikes a parallel-sided block of glass (n = 1.5) at an angle of incidence of 40°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction inside the block. (b) State the angle at which the ray leaves the opposite parallel face, measured from the normal. (c) Explain why the ray changes direction at the first face. (d) Describe how the path would differ if the ray entered along the normal.
items.answer: (a) 25.4° (b) 40° (c) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle. (d) It would pass straight through without bending.
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n (method/substitution) [1]; answer 25.4° with unit [1] [2] (b) 40° [1] (c) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (d) It would pass straight through without bending [1]

items.stem: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels …
options: from air into glass at any angle
from glass into air at an angle greater than the critical angle
from glass into air at an angle less than the critical angle
items.answer: from glass into air at an angle greater than the critical angle
items.markingKey: Needs denser → less dense medium and i > c.

items.stem: Explain why diamonds sparkle more than glass of the same shape.
items.answer: Diamond has a very high refractive index and so a small critical angle (about 24°); light entering is totally internally reflected many times before it leaves.
items.markingKey: high n / small critical angle [1]; many total internal reflections [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how an endoscope lets a doctor see inside a patient’s body.
items.answer: Bundles of optical fibres carry light into the body and carry the reflected image back by total internal reflection, even round bends.
items.markingKey: optical fibres [1]; TIR carries light round bends [1] [2]

items.stem: The refractive index of glass is 1.5. Determine the critical angle.
items.markingKey: sin c = 1/1.5; c = sin⁻¹(1/1.5) = 41.8°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ray inside a block of sapphire (n = 1.77) meets the sapphire–air boundary at an angle of incidence of 50°. Calculate the critical angle and state what happens to the ray.
items.answer: c = 34.4°; total internal reflection.

items.stem: An optical fibre has a core made of Perspex (n = 1.49). (a) Calculate the critical angle of the fibre core. (b) State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection.
items.answer: (a) 42.2° (b) Light travels from a denser to a less dense medium; angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
items.markingKey: (a) sin c = 1/n (method/substitution) [1]; answer 42.2° with unit [1] [2] (b) Light travels from a denser to a less dense medium [1]; angle of incidence greater than the critical angle [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a 45° glass prism can turn a ray through 90° in a periscope.
items.answer: The ray meets the hypotenuse at 45°, which is greater than the critical angle of glass (about 42°), so it is totally internally reflected through 90°.

items.stem: The refractive index of water is 1.33. Calculate the critical angle.
items.markingKey: sin c = 1/1.33; c = sin⁻¹(1/1.33) = 48.8°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In an experiment, the critical angle for a new plastic is measured as 38°. (a) Calculate its refractive index. (b) A ray in the plastic meets the surface at 28°. Calculate the angle of refraction in air. (c) Explain whether this plastic could be used in a 45° prism periscope.
items.answer: (a) 1.62 (b) 49.7° (c) yes: rays hit the long face at 45°, which is greater than the critical angle, so TIR occurs.
items.markingKey: (a) n = 1/sin c [1] = 1.62 [1] (b) sin r = n sin i [1] (c) compare 45° with c [1]; conclusion [1] [5]

items.stem: An optical fibre has a core made of crown glass (n = 1.52). (a) Calculate the critical angle of the fibre core. (b) Give one medical and one communication use of optical fibres.
items.answer: (a) 41.1° (b) Endoscope; broadband/telephone signals.
items.markingKey: (a) sin c = 1/n (method/substitution) [1]; answer 41.1° with unit [1] [2] (b) Endoscope [1]; broadband/telephone signals [1] [2]

items.stem: A converging lens makes parallel rays of light …
options: spread out as if from a point
items.answer: meet at the principal focus
items.markingKey: Converging (convex) lens brings parallel rays to a focus.

items.stem: Describe the three rays used to draw a ray diagram for a converging lens.
items.answer: A ray parallel to the axis refracts through F; a ray through the optical centre passes straight on; a ray through F on the object side emerges parallel to the axis.
items.markingKey: parallel → through F [1]; through centre undeviated [1]; through F → parallel [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a camera with a converging lens produces a real, inverted image on its sensor.
items.answer: The object is far beyond 2F, so rays from it converge to a point beyond F on the other side, forming a real, inverted, diminished image where the sensor is placed.
items.markingKey: object beyond 2F [1]; rays converge to real inverted image [1] [2]

items.stem: An object is placed 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 12 cm. State three properties of the image.
items.answer: Real, inverted, magnified.
items.markingKey: all three properties correct = 2 marks; two correct = 1 mark [2]

items.stem: An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. A scale ray diagram gives the image 60 cm from the lens. Describe the image and calculate its height using magnification = image distance ÷ object distance.
items.answer: Real, inverted, magnified; height 8 cm
items.markingKey: nature [1]; magnification = 60/30 = 2 [1]; height = 8 cm [1] [3]

items.stem: An object 2 cm tall stands on the principal axis 30 cm from a thin converging lens of focal length 20 cm. (a) Describe how to draw a scale ray diagram to locate the image. (b) The diagram gives an image distance of 60 cm. State the nature of the image and where it is. (c) Calculate the image height. (d) Suggest a device that uses this arrangement.
items.answer: (a) choose a scale; draw a ray parallel to the axis then through F; draw a ray through the optical centre undeviated; where they meet is the image. (b) real, inverted, magnified, 60 cm from the lens on the opposite side. (c) 4 cm (d) projector.
items.markingKey: (a) two correct construction rays [1] (b) nature and position [1] (c) magnification method [1] (d) device [1] [4]

items.stem: A thin converging lens has a focal length of 10 cm. (a) An object is placed 30 cm from the lens. Describe the image. (b) Explain why the second image cannot be shown on a screen. (c) Name the arrangement used as a magnifying glass.
items.answer: (a) Real, inverted, diminished, between F and 2F. (b) It is virtual: rays only appear to come from it. (c) Object inside F (less than 10 cm from the lens).
items.markingKey: (a) Real [1]; inverted, diminished, between F and 2F [1] [2] (b) It is virtual: rays only appear to come from it [1] (c) Object inside F (less than 10 cm from the lens) [1]

items.stem: A thin converging lens has a focal length of 10 cm. (a) An object is placed 30 cm from the lens. Describe the image. (b) The object is moved to 5 cm from the lens. Describe the new image. (c) Name the arrangement used as a magnifying glass.
items.answer: (a) Real, inverted, diminished, between F and 2F. (b) Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side as the object. (c) Object inside F (less than 10 cm from the lens).
items.markingKey: (a) Real [1]; inverted, diminished, between F and 2F [1] [2] (b) Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side [1]; as the object [1] [2] (c) Object inside F (less than 10 cm from the lens) [1]

items.stem: The focal length of a lens is the distance from …
options: the centre of the lens to the principal focus
items.answer: the centre of the lens to the principal focus
items.markingKey: f = optical centre to F.

items.stem: Explain how a converging lens acts as a magnifying glass.
items.answer: With the object closer than F, the rays leaving the lens diverge; the eye traces them back to a virtual, upright, magnified image on the same side as the object.
items.markingKey: object inside F [1]; diverging rays traced back → virtual upright enlarged image [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a diverging lens can only form virtual images of real objects.
items.answer: Rays leaving a diverging lens always spread out, so they never meet; they only appear to come from a point on the object side.
items.markingKey: rays always diverge [1]; only appear to meet [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain what causes long sight and how it is corrected with a lens.
items.answer: The eye focuses light from near objects behind the retina (eye lens too weak / eyeball too short); a converging lens converges the rays so they focus on the retina.
items.markingKey: where image forms [1]; correct lens type [1]; how it fixes the focus [1] [3]

items.stem: An object 2 cm tall is placed 24 cm from a converging lens of focal length 12 cm. A scale ray diagram gives the image 24 cm from the lens. Describe the image and calculate its height using magnification = image distance ÷ object distance.
items.answer: Real, inverted, same size; height 2 cm
items.markingKey: nature [1]; magnification = 24/24 = 1 [1]; height = 2 cm [1] [3]

items.stem: A thin converging lens has a focal length of 10 cm. (a) An object is placed 30 cm from the lens. Describe the image. (b) Describe a simple way to measure the focal length.
items.answer: (a) Real, inverted, diminished, between F and 2F. (b) Focus an image of a distant object (window) onto a screen and measure lens–screen distance.
items.markingKey: (a) Real [1]; inverted, diminished, between F and 2F [1] [2] (b) Focus an image of a distant object (window) onto a screen and measure lens–screen distance (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: When white light passes through a prism, which colour is refracted the most?
items.answer: Violet
items.markingKey: Violet has the highest frequency and is slowed most.

items.stem: Dispersion is …
options: the reflection of light from a mirror
the splitting of white light into its component colours
the absorption of light by black surfaces
the bending of light round an obstacle
items.answer: the splitting of white light into its component colours
items.markingKey: Different colours refract by different amounts.

items.stem: Explain why a prism splits white light into a spectrum.
items.answer: White light is a mixture of colours; each colour has a different frequency and travels at a slightly different speed in glass, so each is refracted by a different amount; violet is bent most and red least.
items.markingKey: mixture of colours [1]; different speeds/refractive index [1]; different angles, violet most [1] [3]

items.stem: A type of glass has refractive index 1.510 for red light and 1.529 for violet light. White light enters the glass from air at an angle of incidence of 40°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction for each colour. (b) Explain how this produces a spectrum.
items.answer: (a) red 25.2°, violet 24.9° (b) the colours travel in slightly different directions, so they separate; violet is bent more (smaller r).
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n for each [2] (b) different angles → separation [1] [3]

items.stem: Lina shines sunlight through a prism in a darkened room. (a) State which colour travels slowest in the glass. (b) Describe what is seen if the spectrum passes through a second, inverted prism. (c) Explain why a red laser beam is not split by the prism.
items.answer: (a) Violet. (b) The colours recombine to give white light. (c) It is monochromatic.
items.markingKey: (a) Violet [1] (b) The colours recombine to give white light [1] (c) It is monochromatic [1]

items.stem: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
items.answer: Red
items.markingKey: Red: longest wavelength, lowest frequency.

items.stem: A type of glass has refractive index 1.510 for red light and 1.531 for violet light. White light enters the glass from air at an angle of incidence of 60°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction for each colour. (b) Explain how this produces a spectrum.
items.answer: (a) red 35.0°, violet 34.4° (b) the colours travel in slightly different directions, so they separate; violet is bent more (smaller r).
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n for each [2] (b) different angles → separation [1] [3]

items.stem: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from …
items.answer: the normal
items.markingKey: The normal is perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.

items.stem: Describe how to locate the image of a pin in a plane mirror using ray tracing.
items.answer: Place a pin in front of the mirror; view it from two positions and line up sighting pins with the image each time; draw the lines back behind the mirror; they cross at the image position.
items.markingKey: sighting from two positions [1]; lines extended behind mirror [1]; intersection is image [1] [3]

items.stem: A ray of light makes an angle of 70° with the surface of a plane mirror. State the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection.
items.answer: Both 20°

items.stem: Sofia stands 3 m in front of a large plane mirror in a dance studio. (a) Describe three properties of the image. (b) A ray from the person’s shoe meets the mirror at 35° to the normal. State its angle of reflection. (c) Explain why the image cannot be formed on a screen.
items.answer: (a) Virtual, upright, same size (laterally inverted). (b) 35° (c) Rays do not actually meet there; they only appear to come from behind the mirror.

items.stem: A ray enters a glass block along the normal. What happens to it?
options: It passes straight through without bending
It bends away from the normal
items.answer: It passes straight through without bending
items.markingKey: At 0° incidence there is no change of direction (speed still changes).

items.stem: A ray enters diamond (n = 2.42) and Perspex (n = 1.49) from air at the same angle of incidence of 40°. State in which material it bends more and explain.
items.answer: Diamond: higher refractive index, so light slows more and bends more towards the normal (smaller angle of refraction).
items.markingKey: correct material [1]; higher n → more slowing / smaller r [1] [2]

items.markingKey: n = sin 50° / sin 30° = 1.53. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into ice (refractive index 1.31) with an angle of incidence of 50°. Calculate the angle of refraction.

A ray of light in air strikes a parallel-sided block of Perspex (n = 1.49) at an angle of incidence of 50°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction inside the block. (b) Explain why the ray changes direction at the first face.
items.answer: (a) 30.9° (b) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle.
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n (method/substitution) [1]; answer 30.9° with unit [1] [2] (b) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The critical angle for glass is about 42°. A ray inside the glass meets the surface at 50°. What happens? (b) Optical fibres carry signals using …
items.answer: (a) It is totally internally reflected (b) total internal reflection
items.markingKey: (a) 50° > 42° so TIR. (b) Light reflects repeatedly off the inner surface of the fibre.

items.stem: Explain why optical fibres are used for broadband instead of copper wires.
items.answer: They carry much more data with little loss, are not affected by electrical interference, and are lighter.
items.markingKey: any two advantages [2]

items.stem: The refractive index of crown glass is 1.52. Calculate the critical angle.
items.markingKey: sin c = 1/1.52; c = sin⁻¹(1/1.52) = 41.1°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Explain what causes short sight and how it is corrected with a lens.
items.answer: The eye focuses light from distant objects in front of the retina (eye lens too strong / eyeball too long); a diverging lens spreads the rays so they focus on the retina.
items.markingKey: where image forms [1]; correct lens type [1]; how it fixes the focus [1] [3]

items.stem: An object is placed 45 cm from a converging lens of focal length 15 cm. State three properties of the image.
items.answer: Real, inverted, diminished.
items.markingKey: all three properties correct = 2 marks; two correct = 1 mark [2]

items.stem: An object 3 cm tall is placed 6 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. A scale ray diagram gives the image 15 cm from the lens. Describe the image and calculate its height using magnification = image distance ÷ object distance.
items.answer: Virtual, upright, magnified; height 7.5 cm
items.markingKey: nature [1]; magnification = 15/6 = 2.5 [1]; height = 7.5 cm [1] [3]

items.stem: A thin converging lens has a focal length of 15 cm. (a) An object is placed 45 cm from the lens. Describe the image. (b) The object is moved to 7 cm from the lens. Describe the new image.
items.answer: (a) Real, inverted, diminished, between F and 2F. (b) Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side as the object.
items.markingKey: (a) Real [1]; inverted, diminished, between F and 2F [1] [2] (b) Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side [1]; as the object [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a rainbow is formed.
items.answer: Sunlight enters raindrops and is refracted and dispersed, reflected off the back of the drop, then refracted again as it leaves, spreading the colours out.
items.markingKey: refraction/dispersion in drops [1]; internal reflection [1]; second refraction [1] [3]

items.answer: (a) red 34.9°, violet 34.4° (b) the colours travel in slightly different directions, so they separate; violet is bent more (smaller r).
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n for each [2] (b) different angles → separation [1] [3]

items.stem: A narrow beam of white light passes through a triangular glass prism onto a screen. (a) Name this effect. (b) State which colour appears at the top (least deviated) and which at the bottom. (c) Describe what is seen if the spectrum passes through a second, inverted prism. (d) Explain why a red laser beam is not split by the prism.
items.answer: (a) Dispersion. (b) Red least deviated; violet most. (c) The colours recombine to give white light. (d) It is monochromatic.
items.markingKey: (a) Dispersion [1] (b) Red least deviated [1]; violet most [1] [2] (c) The colours recombine to give white light [1] (d) It is monochromatic [1]

items.stem: The image in a plane mirror is …
options: virtual, upright and the same size as the object
items.answer: virtual, upright and the same size as the object

items.answer: (a) Draw a normal on paper at the mirror; direct rays at different angles of incidence; mark incident and reflected rays; measure both angles from the normal with a protractor and compare. (b) Drivers see it in their rear-view mirrors, which laterally invert the image, so it reads correctly.
items.markingKey: (a) normal drawn [1]; several angles measured with protractor [1]; compare i and r [1] [3] (b) lateral inversion [1]; reads correctly in mirror [1] [2]

items.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 55°. Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray.

Daniel stands 2 m in front of a large plane mirror in a dance studio. (a) State the distance from the person to the image. (b) Describe three properties of the image. (c) A ray from the person’s shoe meets the mirror at 35° to the normal. State its angle of reflection. (d) The person moves 0.5 m closer. State the new distance between person and image.
items.answer: (a) 4 m (b) Virtual, upright, same size (laterally inverted). (c) 35° (d) 3 m
items.markingKey: (a) 4 m [1] (b) Virtual [1]; upright [1]; same size (laterally inverted) [1] [3] (c) 35° [1] (d) 3 m [1]

items.stem: Which equation defines refractive index?
items.answer: n = sin i / sin r
items.markingKey: Ratio of sines of the angles in air (i) and in the medium (r).

items.stem: A ray enters crown glass (n = 1.52) and water (n = 1.33) from air at the same angle of incidence of 40°. State in which material it bends more and explain.
items.answer: Crown glass: higher refractive index, so light slows more and bends more towards the normal (smaller angle of refraction).
items.markingKey: correct material [1]; higher n → more slowing / smaller r [1] [2]

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into crown glass. The angle of incidence is 25° and the angle of refraction is 16°. Calculate the refractive index.
items.markingKey: n = sin 25° / sin 16° = 1.53. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A ray of light passes from air into glass (refractive index 1.5) with an angle of incidence of 20°. Calculate the angle of refraction.

A ray of light in air strikes a parallel-sided block of Perspex (n = 1.49) at an angle of incidence of 50°. (a) Explain why the ray changes direction at the first face. (b) State what happens to the frequency of the light inside the block. (c) Describe how the path would differ if the ray entered along the normal.
items.answer: (a) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle. (b) Unchanged. (c) It would pass straight through without bending.
items.markingKey: (a) It slows down on entering the denser medium at an angle (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) Unchanged [1] (c) It would pass straight through without bending [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) At the critical angle, the refracted ray … (b) Which equation links the critical angle c and refractive index n?
items.answer: (a) travels along the boundary (angle of refraction 90°) (b) n = 1 / sin c
items.markingKey: (a) Definition of the critical angle. (b) sin c = 1/n.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how an endoscope lets a doctor see inside a patient’s body. (b) Explain why a 45° glass prism can turn a ray through 90° in a periscope.
items.answer: (a) Bundles of optical fibres carry light into the body and carry the reflected image back by total internal reflection, even round bends. (b) The ray meets the hypotenuse at 45°, which is greater than the critical angle of glass (about 42°), so it is totally internally reflected through 90°.
items.markingKey: (a) optical fibres [1]; TIR carries light round bends [1] [2] (b) 45° > 42° [1]; TIR turns ray 90° [1] [2]

items.stem: The refractive index of crown glass is 1.52. Work out the critical angle.
items.markingKey: sin c = 1/1.52; c = sin⁻¹(1/1.52) = 41.1°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how a converging lens acts as a magnifying glass. (b) Explain why a camera with a converging lens produces a real, inverted image on its sensor.
items.answer: (a) With the object closer than F, the rays leaving the lens diverge; the eye traces them back to a virtual, upright, magnified image on the same side as the object. (b) The object is far beyond 2F, so rays from it converge to a point beyond F on the other side, forming a real, inverted, diminished image where the sensor is placed.
items.markingKey: (a) object inside F [1]; diverging rays traced back → virtual upright enlarged image [1] [2] (b) object beyond 2F [1]; rays converge to real inverted image [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a camera with a converging lens produces a real, inverted image on its sensor. (b) Explain how a converging lens acts as a magnifying glass.
items.answer: (a) The object is far beyond 2F, so rays from it converge to a point beyond F on the other side, forming a real, inverted, diminished image where the sensor is placed. (b) With the object closer than F, the rays leaving the lens diverge; the eye traces them back to a virtual, upright, magnified image on the same side as the object.
items.markingKey: (a) object beyond 2F [1]; rays converge to real inverted image [1] [2] (b) object inside F [1]; diverging rays traced back → virtual upright enlarged image [1] [2]

items.stem: An object is placed 6 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. State three properties of the image.
items.answer: Virtual, upright, magnified.
items.markingKey: all three properties correct = 2 marks; two correct = 1 mark [2]

items.stem: An object 2 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. A scale ray diagram gives the image 15 cm from the lens. Describe the image and calculate its height using magnification = image distance ÷ object distance.
items.answer: Real, inverted, diminished; height 1 cm
items.markingKey: nature [1]; magnification = 15/30 = 0.5 [1]; height = 1 cm [1] [3]

items.stem: A thin converging lens has a focal length of 15 cm. (a) Define the focal length. (b) The object is moved to 7 cm from the lens. Describe the new image. (c) Name the arrangement used as a magnifying glass.
items.answer: (a) Distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus. (b) Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side as the object. (c) Object inside F (less than 15 cm from the lens).
items.markingKey: (a) Distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus [1] (b) Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side [1]; as the object [1] [2] (c) Object inside F (less than 15 cm from the lens) [1]

items.stem: Explain why no spectrum is seen when laser light passes through a prism.
items.answer: Laser light is monochromatic (one frequency), so there is only one colour to refract and no splitting occurs.
items.markingKey: monochromatic [1]; single angle of refraction [1] [2]

items.stem: A type of glass has refractive index 1.514 for red light and 1.531 for violet light. White light enters the glass from air at an angle of incidence of 50°. (a) Calculate the angle of refraction for each colour. (b) Explain how this produces a spectrum.
items.answer: (a) red 30.4°, violet 30.0° (b) the colours travel in slightly different directions, so they separate; violet is bent more (smaller r).
items.markingKey: (a) sin r = sin i/n for each [2] (b) different angles → separation [1] [3]

items.stem: A narrow beam of white light passes through a triangular glass prism onto a screen. (a) Name this effect. (b) Explain why the colours separate. (c) Describe what is seen if the spectrum passes through a second, inverted prism. (d) Explain why a red laser beam is not split by the prism.
items.answer: (a) Dispersion. (b) Each colour has a different frequency and a different speed (refractive index) in glass, so each refracts by a different amount. (c) The colours recombine to give white light. (d) It is monochromatic.
items.markingKey: (a) Dispersion [1] (b) Each colour has a different frequency and a different speed (refractive index) in glass [1]; so each refracts by a different amount [1] [2] (c) The colours recombine to give white light [1] (d) It is monochromatic [1]
